Businesses must still pay a registered waste collector for the operational service, leaving no clear reason for a micro-firm to buy a separate general-purpose compliance app.

title: DROP deletion orchestration for California data brokers
summary: A managed connector would help California data brokers move DROP deletion lists through identifier standardization, internal data stores, downstream service providers, recurring suppression checks and status reporting without replacing the state's official platform.
rationale: The opportunity qualifies because California data brokers have had to process DROP requests since 1 August 2026, normally at least once every 45 days, and the official workflow requires downloading requests, standardizing and hashing records, matching, deletion and status reporting. The regulations extend the work beyond a simple API call: matched personal information must be deleted, service providers and contractors must be directed to delete, and unmatched requests must be checked against newly collected records before sale or sharing. The identifiable payer is the regulated data broker, while the state supports either an API or manual exchange, creating a narrow wedge for orchestration and evidence across the broker's systems rather than a competing request portal. title: Federal software attestation workspace for US SaaS vendors
summary: A compliance workspace would help smaller software vendors selling to US federal agencies map secure-development evidence to NIST practices, complete a common attestation and reuse the record across procurements.
rationale: The generic opportunity is discarded because its central premise is outdated. OMB Memorandum M-26-05 rescinded the government-wide memoranda that required agencies to obtain secure-software attestations and says agencies are no longer required to collect standardized attestations or use a common form. Agencies may instead tailor risk-based contract terms, while NIST describes the Secure Software Development Framework as recommendations rather than a checklist. CISA still publishes an attestation form, but the form does not restore a uniform mandate. Without a recurring common requirement, the payer, workflow and evidence package fragment by agency and contract, leaving no stable wedge for a general-purpose compliance product.

rationale: The opportunity qualifies because Apple rejects submissions containing invalid privacy manifests and requires valid manifests for commonly used third-party SDKs. The identifiable payer is an app publisher with recurring releases and multiple SDK dependencies. A read-only audit of archived builds can test demand cheaply, and no obvious legal or technical constraint prevents a human-reviewed CI tool that does not submit apps or make legal determinations.

title: 16 KB Android runtime regression gate for app publishers

rationale: The opportunity qualifies because Google Play requires new apps and updates targeting Android 15 or higher to support 16 KB page sizes from 1 February 2027. Google says apps with native code, including native libraries brought in by SDKs, must be rebuilt and tested in a 16 KB environment; its tooling can flag alignment problems, but compatibility mode and static checks do not replace runtime testing. Play's pre-launch report helps detect stability and compatibility issues, yet its automated crawler may not reach every important flow and custom tests are limited. The identifiable payer is an app publisher whose release depends on native SDKs or libraries. The narrow wedge is dependency-change detection plus app-specific 16 KB runtime regression and evidence, not another emulator or app store. A read-only bundle audit and scripted core-flow test can falsify demand cheaply, and no obvious legal or technical constraint prevents a human-reviewed CI service.

title: Trusted-publishing migration workspace for npm package organizations
summary: A managed migration workspace would help organizations with many npm packages inventory legacy publishing credentials, map CI workflows to trusted-publisher configurations, test provenance and preserve rollout evidence before bypass-capable token publishing ends.
rationale: The opportunity qualifies because npm is moving automated publishing from long-lived bypass-capable tokens toward OIDC trusted publishing, with granular access tokens using bypass 2FA no longer accepted for package publication from 1 January 2027. npm's trusted-publishing flow exchanges short-lived credentials from supported CI providers and generates provenance automatically, while its newer support for multiple configurations makes repository, workflow and environment mapping an organization-wide rollout problem rather than a single-package switch. The identifiable payer is a company responsible for publishing and maintaining multiple npm packages. The narrow wedge is cross-package credential inventory, configuration mapping, dry-run validation and exception tracking rather than another registry or CI platform. A read-only audit of package settings and workflow files can test demand cheaply, and no obvious legal or technical constraint prevents a human-reviewed migration service.

title: MCP security regression gate for enterprise agent teams
industry: AI agent security and developer tooling
summary: A vendor-neutral release gate would help teams deploying MCP-connected agents detect tool-schema drift, overbroad permissions, unsafe approval settings and prompt-injection data paths before production releases.
rationale: The opportunity qualifies because MCP-connected agents can expose sensitive context to malicious servers and can be induced by untrusted content to leak data or take unintended actions. OWASP identifies tool poisoning, post-approval tool-definition changes, excessive permissions and cross-server escalation, and recommends hashing complete tool definitions, reviewing changes and preserving explicit invocation approval. The identifiable payer is an enterprise team deploying agents that can reach business systems. The narrow wedge is a vendor-neutral CI and predeployment regression gate that snapshots schemas and scopes, checks approval policy and replays synthetic injection scenarios across local and remote MCP integrations rather than another runtime firewall. Microsoft's preview MCP firewall confirms demand for centralized controls but is tied to its network and identity stack, leaving room for portable release testing. A read-only audit and synthetic replay can test demand cheaply, and no obvious legal or technical constraint prevents a harness that uses test credentials and executes no production actions.
